titleStmt.title: MetaH Support for Real-Time Multi-Processor Avionics

analytic.title: MetaH Support for Real-Time Multi-Processor Avionics

application.desc: GROBID - A machine learning software for extracting information from scholarly documents

div.p: MetaH is a language for describing the software and hardware architecture of real-tame fault-tolerant securely partitioned avionics systems The MetaH toolset supports, among other things, real-time sehedulability analysis and the automatic generation of "glue" code that implements real-time message passing and process dispatching for a class of multi-processor target architectures We describe the development methodology and typacal requirements that motivated the language and tools We give an overview of the message and process scheduling methods used in the current toolset and briefly discuss research to extend this approach to larger-scale distributed systems such as fire control and air trafic control 'This work has been supported by DARPA and ONR under contract N00014-91-C-0195

div.head: Introduction
div.p: The development of avionics systems requires the talents of many engineers trained in a variety of disciplines, of which software engineering is only one There are trends towards more concurrent and iterative multi-disciplinary development, towards greater reuse of a variety of development artifacts, and towards greater automation and increased use of specialized tools We will first discuss the development context assumed by our work Different kinds of systems impose different kinds of real-time requirements Our work initially focused on systems that provide guidance, navigation and feedback control functions, although we must allow for other kinds of functionality as well (e g display generation, on-board data base management) We will outline some requirements that impacted the choices we made for real-time scheduling and resource allocation We will then discuss some of the additional capabilities that would be required in wider-area distributed applications such as fire control After presenting the development context and assumed requirements, we will give an overview of an architecture definition language we have developed for real-time fault-tolerant securely partitioned multiprocessor systems This language, called MetaH, has an associated toolset that automates several analysis and implementation tasks In this paper we will focus in particular on the resource allocation and scheduling methods used for periodic processes and messages in multi-processor systems We discuss the technologies used in our current toolset and identify areas of current research intended to address a broader set of requirements, e g a distributed fire control system We close with a discussion of some recent research in these areas

div.head: Software Architectures
div.p: The study of software architectures has become increasingly popular in recent years[lO, 361 Although no consensus definition has emerged, there is general agreement that a specification of a software architecture explains how a complex software system is built from subprogram-sized or larger modules, and the mechanisms by which control and data flow between these modules A software architecture description can be viewed as a kind of software design specification One interesting idea to emerge from research on software architectures is the concept of "architecture style " An architecture style is a kind of design idiom or methodology, e g client-server, data flow, blackboard In our work we have been particularly interested in architecture styles that have associated formal modeling and analysis methods as well as associated implementation methods Our working definition of architecture style includes three main elements: notations for describing architectures developed in that style, methods for producing associated formal models from an architecture description, and methods for producing an implementation from an architecture description Our formal architecture styles are initially constructed from existing theory that has proven useful to address various engineering issues For example, a block diagram style useful for guidance, navigation and control can be based on linear and dynamical systems theory Concurrent process theory and real-time scheduling theory can also serve as bases for architecture styles The distinction between an architecture style and a formal modeling theory alone is that a style integrates design notation and methods for producing an implementation together with methods for producing a formal model The translation from notation to formal models and implementation should preserve important structure There should be welldefined and intuitive mappings between the three to increase assurance of correctness and support development tasks such as change management, requirements traceability, structured testing and debugging There is no single style (as we have defined style here) that is sufficiently powerful to address all the engineering issues that arise when building a complex system Consequently, we must have an approach that allows us to use many different styles to describe, analyze and implement a complex software system The notations and tools used for a particular class of requirements and functions are sometimes called domain-specific, since they are specialized for a particular set of needs and would not normally be used outside of that domain of applicability Figure 1 illustrates how we deal with this using some of the tools we have developed

ControlH is based on a block diagram style and is used by guidance, navigation and control (GN&C) engineers to specify, analyze and generate code for functions such as autopilots and vehicle controllers [8] ControlH is only one example of a domain-specific language and toolset In general, a collection of specialized tools will need to be integrated that depends on the particular kinds of products an organization produces Display management, data base management, and communications are all examples of kinds of functions for which domain-specific toolsets have been produced[35, 2, 11 DoME is a meta-CASE tool that supports the rapid production of graphical user interfaces for design tools and the rapid production of simple tools that traverse graphical design specifications and generate artifacts from them [22] DoME is somewhat analogous to a set of compiler compiler tools for a graphical language Given a graphical syntax, the metaDoME tool can automatically generate a graphical editor for that graphical language, code to maintain an associated internal data structure, and an application programming interface that makes it easy to write specialized back-end tools in an associated scripting language MetaH, our software and hardware architecture specification language and toolset, is used to compose modules obtained from the domain-specific toolsets (or written by hand or re-engineered from existing code [24]) to produce the final load images for a system MetaH performs analysis for systems-level properties such as real-time schedulability and reliability, generates "glue code" to combine all the functional code modules, and manages the overall build process Resource allocation and real-time scheduling (like reliability and safety/security) are system-wide issues since they potentially involve all source modules and hardware resources in a system These issues are primarily dealt with using the MetaH software and systems integration language and toolset The primary focus of this paper is on MetaH, how it performs realtime scheduling in multi-processor systems, and the interaction between MetaH and the domain-specific tools used to produce a set of functional modules

div.head: Requirements
div.p: Avionics systems are moving away from federated systems in which each function has a dedicated processor towards integrated systems in which multiple functions are hosted on a multi-processor This significantly reduces logistics and maintenance costs, reduces size/weight/power, and makes it easier to upgrade functionality through software changes alone[l'T, 211 Integrated avionics software is functionally heterogeneous. Most of the workload consists of multiple and diverse functions (e g autopilot, navigation, data bases, diagnostics) However, some functions will increasingly be implemented using parallel algorithms (e g guidance and route planning, image processing and display generation) We expect most on-board integrated modular avionics systems will be of modest size relative to massively parallel computers (e g tens rather than thousands of processors), and any parallelism will be relatively course-grained e g a few parrather than thousands of parallel operations of a few microseconds each).

Integrated avionics systems must support secure partitioning[l7, 18 Different functions in an avionics of criticality, e g safety-critical, mission-critical, noncritical The higher the criticality level is, the more extensive and expensive the certification process is Rather than certify all software to the highest level at great cost, each function can be certified to the level required if the system guarantees that no defect in a less-critical function can possibly disrupt the execution of a more-critical function This is essentially a security requirement, where the executive must not only provide data protection (space partitioning) but also protection against disruption of real-time scheduling (time partitioning) An executive must provide memory protection, must limit the capabilities of certain processes to make certain service requests, and must insure that high-criticality scheduling events that can be observed externally (e g messages) cannot be affected by any lower-criticality process behavior This trend towards greater levels of integration is expected to go beyond on-board systems, e g air vehicles will have direct digital links to the air traffic control system and will be viewed as complex mobile nodes within that distributed system This will probably occur in incremental steps For example, the existence of a physical link between an on-board and a ground-based system does not mean they are fully integrated in the sense an application developer is provided with a uniform development methodology and environment and can easily choose how to partition functionally across the two Fundamental differences in development methods and design and implementation may still exist (e g hard versus soft real-time Physical links may be visible to the developer as litt 1 e scheduling, error masking versus dynamic recovery more than devices in the two systems Our interest is in a reasonably well-integrated approach applied uniformly across a large set of processors and application functions and domains

We initially focused on guidance, navigation and control (GN&C) functions We developed ControlH, a language and toolset for design, analysis and implementation of GN&C models and algorithms. Con-trolH is based on the block diagram notation widelyused in this field and can be thought of as a specialized allel tasks that execute for several mil \ iseconds each, systems are typica 1 ly classified to be of different levels -I- In the idealized synchronous model, two processes are dispatched simultaneously at any instant of time where the shorter period evenly divides the longer period, and the most recent output messages of a process are transferred to the receiving process when the receiving process is dispatched. This means the communication must occur between the completion of the producing process and the start of the consuming process. Where values pass between processes of different rates they are undersampled or oversampled as appropriate. We take it as a scheduling requirement that the results of a GN&C function should be the same no matter how the processes are distributed across multiple processors. Although periodic hard real-time processing is the basis of most GN&C functions, many other avionics functions require aperiodic (event-driven) processing.
For hard real-time aperiodics, a lower bound must be mandated for event inter-arrival times and an upper bound must be mandated for process execution times.

Polling has been widely-used in the past, but periodic polling incurs overhead, and dispatch (and consequently response) times may be delayed by as much as the polling period. Aperiodic event arrivals cause run-time variations in CPU demand, but such variations also occur due to variable process execution times. Scheduling methods should efficiently, reliably and predictably support both hard real-time periodic time Figure 2: GN&C Periodic Processing Timeline and aperiodic processes (deadlines must be guaranteed) and soft real-time periodic and aperiodic processes (response times need not always be less than some fixed deadline). Processes of different criticalities must be supported so that system functionality can degrade gracefully during periods of system overload.
We take it as a requirement that there must be a formal basis for modeling, analyzing and verifying the schedulability of systems that provide critical functions.

Most avionics systems need to be able to dynamically reconfigure themselves to some degree. Current aircraft avionics systems often alter the set of active functions using normal if-then-else control constructs in the source code. Fault-tolerant aircraft avionics typically use error masking alone, but longmission spacecraft do employ dynamic reconfiguration strategies. This is partly due to the greater difficulty of developing and certifying dynamically reconfigurable systems and partly due to different mission requirements (ultra-reliable operation for hours ver-sus moderately reliable operation for years) Only a few vehicles require that it be possible to update software in-flight (e g satellites), but this is needed for ground-based systems that have high availability requirements We feel it will be necessary to support some level of dynamic reconfiguration at the scheduling and resource allocation level for both functional reconfiguration (i e to change the set of processes and corresponding functions that are active), resource reconfiguration (i e to change the scheduling and resource allocation solution currently in effect), and eventually on-line system upgrade (i e change or add functions to the system) On-board systems impose stricter size, weight and power constraints than ground-based systems This tends to favor simple and specialized software solutions Another factor that has traditionally favored simple specialized solutions is the need to certify avionics software to high levels of assurance in some cases Testing and verification and validation typically account for over half the cost of avionics software development Even though an integrated modular avionics approach can reduce the certification cost for a p plication functions, the core IMA infrastructure must still be certified to the highest levels and so should be as simple and verifiable as possible [34]

div.head: MetaH Overview
div.p: MetaH is a language for specifying software and hardware architectures for real-time, securely partitioned, fault-tolerant, scalable multi-processor systems MetaH allows developers to specify how a system is composed from software components like processes and packages and hardware components like processors and memories An associated toolset performs syntactic and semantic checks and also other functions such as realrtime schedulability analysis and application composition Figure 3 shows the current toolset MetaH is somewhat like an integration of a CASE toolset, a modeling and analysis toolset, and a development environment for a real-time operating system Unlike a traditional CASE toolset, MetaH assumes the functional modules are produced externally and focuses on non-functional aspects like timing, reliability, security, and software and software/hardware composition and integration. MetaH provides no separate modeling languages, but instead automatically generates various formal models from the architectural specification MetaH does a significant amount of analysis and optimization off-line, producing executables that are smaller, faster and less subject to certain classes of defects than hand-written integration code executing on a real-time operating system Although MetaH can be targeted to a traditional real-time operating system, in spirit it is more like a compiler than an interpreter, since operations like process and mailbox creation are largely done off-line and extensive static checking is performed Low-level software constructs of the MetaH language describe source components written in some traditional programming language like Ada MetaH subprogram, package and monitor specifications describe important attributes of source modules such as the file containing the source code, nominal and maximum compute times on various kinds of processors, stack and heap requirements, real-time semaphore protocol to be used, etc Events (user-specified enumeration literals used in certain service calls) and ports (buffer variables used to hold message values) can appear within source modules and must be described in the MetaH specification

The higher-level constructs of the MetaH language are processes, macros and modes Processes group together source modules that are to be scheduled as either periodic or aperiodic processes A process is also the basic unit of security and fault containment, and memory protection and compute time enforcement are provided Macros and modes group processes, define connections between events and ports, and define equivalences between packages and modules that are to be shared between processes The difference is that macros run in parallel with each other, while modes are mutually exclusive Event connections between modes are used to define hierarchical mode transition diagrams, where mode changes at run-time can stop or start processes or change connections MetaH also allows hardware architectures to be specified using memory, processor, channel, and device components grouped into systems Hardware objects may have ports, events or monitors in their interfaces Software and hardware ports and events can be connected to each other, and software can access hardware monitors (hardware monitors provide hardwaredependent service calls) Hardware descriptions identify (among other things) hardware-dependent source code modules for device drivers, and code to provide a standard interface between automatically composed applications and the underlying real-time operating system.

Both graphical and textual specification is supported The two can be mixed (part of a specification can be maintained textually and part graphically), and the toolset can translate graphical to textual and vice versa This is convenient in a software and systems integration tool, since different parts of a specification may be produced by different groups or automatically generated by different domain-specific tools A simple software/hardware binding tool assigns to hardware those software objects in a specification that are not explicitly assigned, possibly subject to userspecified constraints An executive generator tool automatically produces the "glue" code needed to compose the various source modules to form the overall application This glue code resembles an application-specific executive or supervisor, with code to dispatch processes and pass messages, synchronize access to shared resources, vector events, perform mode changes, etc

The design schema for the generated executives is based on preemptive fixed priority scheduling theory Using attributes in MetaH specifications of process period, preperiod deadline and criticality, the executive generator derives priority, period transformation, and dispatch and time slice refill information used in data tables and dispatching code Port connection specifications and process timing information are used to schedule and generate code to move data between processes' port buffer variables Monitor specifications are used to generate semaphore protocol and timing data tables Code to vector events to dispatch aperiodics or to trigger mode changes, and code to manage mode changes, is also generated We will discuss the multi-processor aspects of this executive in greater detail in the next section Using information contained in the MetaH specification and produced by the executive generator, the real-time modeler generates a detailed preemptive fixed priority schedulability model of the application The model contains elements common to all applications (e g a dispatcher process) and elements that are application-dependent (e g process periods and compute times, monitor blocking times, communication times) The model includes all scheduling and communication overheads and is a conservative and accurate representation of the final load image structure and behavior (from the real-time scheduling viewpoint)

The schedulability analysis algorithm we currently use is an extension of the exact characterization algorithm [33] Our analysis tool produces sensitivity analysis information describing how compute times may be changed while preserving (or in order to achieve) schedule feasibility; and it allows processes to be decomposed into component source modules and provides timing analysis data for individual source modules

The MetaH language includes a construct called an error model, which allows users to specify sets of fault events and error states An error model also includes specifications of transition functions to define how the error states of objects change due to fault, error propagation and recovery events. An individual object within a specification can then be annotated to specify the error transition function and fault arrival rates for that object

We have a prototype reliability modeling tool that generates a stochastic concurrent process reliability model[l5, 291 Error propagations between objects are modeled as synchronizations or rendezvous between stochastic concurrent processes Each such propagation synchronization in the model can be controlled using an associated consensus expression, which can conditionally mask propagations depending on the current error states of selected objects In the MetaH specification, user-supplied consensus expressions describe the error detection protocols that are implemented by the underlying source modules for a particular application The reliability modeler uses the MetaH error model specifications and annotations to generate the proper set of object error state machines, and uses the consensus expressions and design structure to generate the proper set of propagation synchronizations between these object error state machines A subset of the reachable state space of this stochastic concurrent process is a Markov chain that can be analyzed using existing tools and techniques[l5, 201. We selected a stochastic concurrent process model rather than one of the more popular stochastic Petri Net [7, 281 models because it allows us to generate a reliability model whose structure can be easily traced back to the MetaH specification and vice versa (recall that maintaining good mappings be-'The reliability modeler does not currently support multiple modes of operation and does not perform any Markov state space reduction optimizations tween specification, formal models and code is one of our goals)

The executive code generated from a MetaH specification includes a number of security mechanisms (protected process address spaces, process criticalities, enforcement of execution time limits, capability lists for executive services) We have a prototype safety/security modeling and analysis tool to check that the mechanisms properly enforce a particular safety or security policy We have currently identified one safety policy and one security policy to be checked

We allow source objects to be annotated with a safety level to indicate the degree to which the code has been assured correct[lB] The safety policy is that proper operation of an object cannot be affected by an error in any other object having a lower safety level For example, a higher-criticality object should not receive data from a lower-criticality object (unless thc connection is explicitly annotated in the MetaH specification to allow this) A higher-criticality process must have a higher scheduling criticality specified than all lower-criticality processes on the same processor, or else execution times must be enforced on all lower-criticality processes on the same processor Objects might also be annotated with a list of security rights The security policy is that an object cannot receive or share data unless it has at least the security rights of the object that supplies the data The connections or data accesses of an object with many security rights can be annotated in the MetaH specification to show that only some subset of these rights are needed to access information provided through that particular connection or shared data area, however Security (and safety) properties can also be specified for hardware objects, e g an inter-processor channel can be flagged as low-security (or low-criticality), making it erroneous to route a high-security (or highcriticality) message over that channel

The MetaH system is similar to a number of others such as Durra 31, Maruti [27], SARTOR [25], ABE 1 4 , LileAnna 1 311, CAPS [23] and Onika/Chimera [ I 11 in its use of an architectural specification language for composing source modules written in a traditional programming language It is similar to Real-Time Euclid [30], Maruti, SARTOR, CAPS and Onika/Chimera in its integration of real-time schedulability theory and analysis with automated code generation or composition Modes and macros [32] pro- vide capabilities to specify hierarchical system-level state transitions that are comparable to aspects of Durra, Statemate [13] and Modechart [19] MetaH represents a selection, integration and extension of a variety of basic technologies in an attempt to meet the requirements of a range of real-time fault-tolerant securely partitioned multi-processor applications

div.head: Multi-Processor Scheduling
div.p: The MetaH toolset currently supports multiprocessor architectures having the following two properties 'Security checks are not currently implemented 1 All processors must receive a nearly-synchronous clock interrupt whose period evenly divides all application process periods (typically the clock interrupt period equals the smallest application process period) This is usually provided by a common fault-tolerant hardware clock and associated interrupt circuitry, although it could be provided in software using a distributed clock protocol All message passing and process dispatching is performed by an automatically generated handler for this interrupt 2 Inter-processor transmission and propagation times are small enough relative to processor speed that sending processors can block awaiting an acknowledgement from receiving processors Such communication is often provided by a common memory bus, or by connecting processors pairwise in some topology using dual-port memories All inter-processor message passing is performed by automatically generated code that copies messages into send buffers, releases the buffers for transmission, then awaits receipt of corresponding buffers from other processors Before proceeding with a more detailed discussion of multi-processor scheduling and communication, we note that the toolset fixes a software-to-hardware binding before generating scheduling and communication code By the time message and process scheduling is performed, all process-to-processor, messageto-channel routing, and shared data-to-memory binding decisions have been made. Mode changes can be used to stop an instance of a process on one processor and start another instance on another processor, or to switch to a different routing of messages over channels or between multiple redundant instances of processes, but a mode change cannot migrate a specific instance of a process and its internal state from one processor to another Similarly, the toolset does not currently support systems in which multiple processors share a single process ready queue MetaH message passing is implemented by moving data between user-specified buffer variables that are called port variables Source modules that send or receive messages are written as if their input values appear in statically allocated port variables and compute their output values into statically allocated port variables Each port variable in a source module is described by a port declaration in the MetaH specification, and port-to-port connections in the MetaH specification will result in executive code being generated to move values between the connected port variables at run-time All moves into (out of a port varidispatch) of the containing process Figure 4 illustrates the timeline for communication and process scheduling In the current executive, the code responsible for periodically dispatching processes includes assignments between processes' port variables (all memory pages containing port variables are mapped into the virtual address space of the generated executive) Port-to-port assignments are per-able must occur after the deadline (be 1 ore the next process release time process period and / imdicit deadline - formed immediately before any associated process dispatches, which are blocked until the inter-process communication completes. If a connection is between two harmonic processes on the same processor, a single assignment directly from the output port variable to the input port variable can be executed immediately before the dispatch of the process having the lowest period. Otherwise, an intermediate variable must be allocated in the executive to hold the value between the deadline of the sending process and the dispatch of the receiving process, and/or inter-processor communication code must be generated to move values between processors. Appropriate conditional statements must also be included to handle error conditions (e.g. process overrun).

Data moves between port variables are nonpreemptively scheduled by the MetaH toolset. However, process scheduling is performed using preemptive fixed priority (rate monotonic) scheduling. What the toolset does is statically schedule data moves and process dispatches. A handler for the periodic clock in-terrupt is generated to perform these periodic actions. Once dispatched, a process is preemptively scheduled according to its priority.

Run-time scheduling of periodic actions (port-toport assignments and periodic process dispatches) is driven by a periodic hardware clock interrupt. At each interrupt a cycle counter is incremented by 1 (modulo some large value to avoid overflow), with the periodic scheduling actions that are to occur at an interrupt determined by whether or not the cycle counter is evenly divisible by the periodicity of each action. Figure 5 illustrates the scheduling control construct currently being generated, which is executed as part of a non-preemptable clock interrupt handler. Scheduling actions (port-to-port assignments and process dispatches) are inserted in the appropriate if-then statement or case statement case, depending on the period of those actions.

Let P I , P2, ..., Pn be the periods of the processes to be scheduled, expressed as integer multiples of the hardware clock interrupt period (this is a restriction. enforced by the toolset). By convention, PI 5 P2 5 ... 5 P,, where Pi is the period of process i. Within a given mode, the scheduling actions taken at a particular interrupt depend on the value of CYCLE in Figure 5. CYCLE keeps count of the number of clock interrupts received modulo Q, where Q is a common multiple of all periods in the application. Scheduling actions that are to occur with some periodicity Pi are executed whenever CYCLE mod Pi = 0.

The structure shown in Figure 5 has the property that all actions to be executed at some periodicity Pi are grouped together (where the actions executed at periodicity Pi < Pj, Pi evenly divides Pj , are a subset of those executed at Pj). This is in contrast, for example, to the use of multiple if-then statements (one for each period), or multiple case statements (one for each subset of periods that has a reasonably small least common multiple). This allows all port-to-port assignments that are to be performed at a clock interrupt to be grouped into one contiguous list and ordered for more efficient execution.

The construct shown handles large ranges of process periods efficiently, providing the periods are strictly harmonic beyond some period Qj . The if-then statements are intended for those processes which are periodic but infrequently executed, and their inclusion can significantly reduce the size of the case statement. Qj is the least common multiple of P I , Pz, ..., Pj, and Qj, Pj+l, ..., P, are strictly harmonic (each period evenly divides all greater periods). A port-toport assignment or process dispatch with periodicity P 5 Qj is placed in every if-then statement and every Pth case of the case statement. A port-to-port assignment or process dispatch with periodicity P > Qj is placed in every if-then statement whose periodicity Pj is >_ P .

Figure 6 provides a somewhat abstracted illustration of the inter-processor communication protocol used between a pair of adjacent processors. At each global clock interrupt, all processors begin executing their respective versions of this sequence (which de- Each channel (the MetaH term for a piece of hardware that supports inter-processor communication) must provide an associated I/O buffer for each pair of processors connected to that channel. One processor sends to another by moving data into a buffer associated with a channel then releasing that buffer for transmission. If a channel supports memory sharing, the channel buffer is just a block of shared memory and the buffer can be released by setting a flag.

Each processor is assigned initial ownership of one half of the channel buffer connecting it to each adjacent processor (the toolset does this offline when processing the hardware architecture specification). The generated executive code on each processor knows whether it starts its protocol at each clock interrupt as the owner of the low or the high half of each channel buffer. Each buffer half has an associated ownership flag, and each processor resets these flags as the very first step in the communication protocol. Every processor sets both flags in order to provide tolerance to lost or delayed clock interrupts. The first two operations shown in Figure 6 for processors A and B represent these operations, where the names l o and h i refer to the low and high halves of the channel buffer.

The first phase of every communication exchange is always the exchange of executive state information between processors. This is the first input of Figure 6. Once a processor moves a copy of its state information into the channel buffer half it owns, it enters a busywait that transfers ownership of its half to the connected processor and awaits ownership of the other half. This is represented in Figure 6 by the repeat loop. At the conclusion of this exchange, pointers to all received state informatlon are passed to a consensus protocol module (which can be easily replaced to adapt to application reliability requirements).

As illustrated in Figure 6, this sequence of exchanges of buffer halves between processors continues for as many phases as needed to perform all the communication at that clock interrupt between all processors. The number of phases depends on the hardware topology (the maximum number of channels a message must be routed through between any pair of processors) and on the sizes of the channel buffers and the amount of data to be transferred.

The temporal formulas in Figure 6 show conditions that hold during particular intervals of the protocol, the intervals between the horizontal lines. Thus, the temporal formula Olo.own = A means that processor A always owns the low buffer half throughout the copy of data to or from that buffer, but this condition only holds up to the repeat statement. The temporal formula 0hi.own = A means that as the repeat loop executes, eventually A will receive ownership of the high half of the buffer. These temporal formulas assume, of course, that there are no faults.

The actual code that awaits a buffer half includes a timeout value to make the protocol tolerant to clock or adjacent processor faults. If any await times out, or if an error is detected in the received data, then an associated channel strike counter is incremented and the channel is marked as having a channel error. No further communication via that channel will be attempted at this clock interrupt, but this error flag will be reset after this cycle and communication will be attempted at subsequent clock interrupts. However, if too many near-coincident channel errors are detected then the channel is marked as failed (unless and until the application software explicitly re-initializes the system). Copies to and from the buffer halves, awaits on buffers, and checks on channel buffer validity, must be made within conditional control constructs in order to avoid accessing channels flagged as erroneous or failed. The error-handling code must also mimic the timing of skipped communications in order to maintain proper timing with respect to the other channels.

The protocol code is further complicated when a processor has more than one other adjacent processor. The channel buffer assignments within a phase must be grouped according to the channel buffers they access for error handling purposes. Groups of assignments are ordered in a way that allows a processor to release buffers as soon as possible, which can increase concurrency among all the processors involved. If a processor is merely an intermediate along a data route, a direct assignment cannot always be generated from one channel buffer to another. An intermediate temporary buffer is sometimes needed, analogous to the intermediate variable needed when swapping the values of two variables.

The mechanics of sharing port variables and laying out channel buffers are worth mentioning. The techniques used allow the generated executive code to be fairly independent of the compiler-specific memory layout chosen for variables, which makes it much easier to retar et the toolset to different compilers and processors fanother of our goals).

When a MetaH specification is processed, the tools parse any source files declared to contain port vari-ables or port types (MetaH strongly types ports, but allows the types to be declared using the underlying programming language with some restrictions). A check is made to insure that declared variables and types actually appear in the source code, and copies of these declarations are included with the generated executive code. Application code and executive code thus contain identical port type and port variable declarations. Linker commands are used to assign corresponding port variable declarations to the same physical location.

After a schedule of communication assignments has been produced, the tools know which values need to be transmitted by each processor over each channel at each phase. A record is declared for each processor for each channel for each phase. These records contain fields for every message to be transmitted by that processor at that time and are the buffers sent between processors. In the current implementation, a replaceable target-specific routine is called to initialize access (pointer) variables to the appropriate record types for each channel buffer. Target and compiler-dependent checks and physical buffer allocation are performed by this target-specific routine, which is called only during system start or re-start.

The algorithm used to schedule inter-processor assignments first expands each connection into a sequence of assignments between port variables and channel buffer variables. For example, a connection between two port variables that must pass through an intermediate processor may expand into as many as five assignments: from a port variable to a channel buffer variable (executed on the processor hosting the sending process), from a channel buffer variable to a temporary variable (executed on the intermediate processor), from the temporary variable to a channel buffer variable (executed on the intermediate processor), from a channel buffer variable to a temporary variable executed on the processor hosting the porary variable to the port variable (executed on the processor hosting the receiving process).

The connections are sorted according to the length of the associated sequence of assignments and then packed into phases according to message size and the processor that is to execute each assignment. Within each phase, a natural sort based on a complex precedence relation is used to order and group assignments to meet requirements for fault tolerance, interprocessor hand-shaking, etc. The overall a1 orithm is reminiscent of a blend of first-fit decreasing fa theoretically reasonable bin-packing algorithm) and longest path first (a theoretically reasonable algorithm for parallelizing acyclic task graphs)[9, 161. This allows us to schedule assignments rapidly while at the same time producing a hopefully reasonably good solution.

We wanted to make it feasible to invoke the tools in an iterative fashion during design studies, which means the execution time of the tools must be reasonable. We elected to use relatively fast heuristics that theory suggests would produce reasonably good answers for both software/hardware binding and interprocessor communication scheduling, avoiding such receiving non-i armonic process), and from the tem-techniques as simulated annealing or genetic optimization. To give one benchmark, a synthetic specification containing 240 connections between 120 processes targeted t o a 16 node hypercube can be parsed, bound, scheduled, and have a schedulability analysis performed in about 4 minutes of Sparc 20 CPU time.

div.head: Future Research
div.p: Blocking the processors to perform inter-processor communication over high-bandwidth low-latency channels imposes reasonably small execution-time overhead. To give one benchmark, a few years ago Honeywell prototyped an avionics system having 7 processors connected pair-wise by 7 dual-port memories in an application-specific topology. The system was scheduled and programmed by hand using an approach similar to that outlined in this paper. The message passing overhead (including all interprocessor synchronization overhead) was estimated to be between 5-10% of processor throughput. We conjecture that the execution time of our automaticallygenerated code may have been less, since (in order to keep the scheduling problem tractable) the original hand-developed schedule transmitted all messages at every clock interrupt, regardless of the periods of the sending or receiving process.

However, more hardware-efficient systems could be built using channels of lower bandwidth. More widely distributed systems have a significant latency that is independent of bandwidth. This will require switching to a more sophisticated distributed scheduling approach that allows a message transmission, once it has been "dispatched" on the inter-processor channel, to take place concurrently with processor execution. Unfortunately, traditional approaches to solving the hard real-time distributed or end-to-end scheduling problem may not be tractable for large systems. For example, the University of Maryland applied a simulated annealing approach to solve a sanitized version of the hard real-time scheduling problem for the 6-node Boeing 777 Aircraft Information Management System, which took about 20 hours on a DEC Alpha [6]. We have investigated a decomposition approach similar in spirit to that reported by GutiQrez et. al. in which an intermediate set of deadlines and release times for the computations and messa es in an end-to-end sequence are iteratively computedfl2]. They report solving an 8 processor, 3 bus, 50 process scheduling problem in roughly 10 seconds, versus roughly 150 minutes for simulated annealing. Our preliminary experience, using a different set of iteration equations, supports their results. For example, we were able to schedule and analyze a singlebus, 480 processor, 8400 process system in about 3.5 minutes on a Sparc 20.

The existing toolset uses a relatively simple algorithm (the deferred server) to support aperiodic processes. We are currently upgrading our aperiodic scheduling and analysis to utilize emerging slack scheduling techniques[26, 41. Slack scheduling was originally developed to provide more rapid response times and more efficiently scheduling for aperiodic processes. Slack scheduling can support several classes of aperiodic processes in the same inte-grated system, ranging from hard-deadline aperiodics with bounded computation and interarrival times to soft-deadline aperiodics with varying computation and interarrival times. Slack scheduling methods should also be applicable to incremental processes, designto-time processes, and period transformation of processes. We prototyped a real-time implementation of slack scheduling of aperiodic processes by modifying a MetaH-generated application. These results, together with a paper study of a commercial avionics executive, suggest context swap times are increased by 10-40%, which is quite reasonable for many applications [5]. Our ultimate goal is to support a broad range of process types, ranging from critical hard real-time through nonessential soft real-time, in the same integrated system.

The toolset currently enumerates reachable modes of operation off-line. A transition mode, in which process starts and stops etc. are scheduled, is introduced for each possible transition in the MetaH specification [32]. Each of these modes is scheduled and analyzed by the tools. A run-time mode change is performed by having all processors simultaneously (at the same clock interrupt) switch to the desired precomputed, pre-analyzed transition mode and thence to the new user-specified operating mode. However, additional work is needed to synchronize mode changes with process scheduling in a way that meets specific application requirements. For example, restricting mode changes so they occur only at the hyperperiod of the processes in the current and next mode provides a cleaner semantics for message passing and slack scheduling. We also need to allow user-specified voting on mode changes to tolerate faults that might erroneously trigger mode changes, and we need to provide mechanisms to resynchronize the mode of a processor that has been restarted due to a transient fault. For on-line upgrades, we would need to extend the toolset to down-load a new set of modes in background and reclaim the resources of modes that no longer appear in an upgraded MetaH specification.

In this paper we described an approach to systems development that allows a variety of domainspecific tools and subsystems to be integrated into a complex system, and closely couples architectural specification and formal modeling and analysis and implementation. Our initial toolset focused on hard real-time, fault-tolerant, securely partitioned, multiprocessor on-board avionics GN&C systems. However, we feel the general approach is broadly applicable, and we are pursuing research in areas that would allow us to extend our languages and tools to more widely distributed systems hosting more complex realtime workloads.
